title: Existence & Uniqueness
text:
Before we try to analyze a inital value problem like: \[\frac{dy}{dt}=f(t,y), \quad y(t_0)=y_0\] using a qualitative or numerical approach, it is important to know the answer to two questions:

Does a solution exist?
Are solutions unique?

Answering yes to the first question means that there is a function \(y(t)\) defined on some open interval \(I\subset \mathbb R\) containing \(t_0\) that satisfies both the initial condition and the differential equation for all \(t\) in the interval \(I\).
The following example illustrates what can go wrong.



Explain why the initial value problem (note how it is written a different way!): \[y\cdot\frac{dy}{dt}-1 = 0, \quad y(t_0)=y_0\] has no solution when \(y_0=0\).
Explain why the initial value problem: \[\frac{dy}{dt}=\text{sign}(t), \quad y(t_0)=y_0\] has no solution when \(t_0=0\).







TipAnswer:






Rewriting the equation as \(y\cdot\frac{dy}{dt}=1\), notice that if \(y(t_0)=y_0=0\), then plugging into the equation gives \[0\cdot\frac{dy}{dt}\bigg\rvert_{t_0} = 0 \ne 1\] no matter what value \(\frac{dy}{dt}\bigr\rvert_{t_0}\) takes. So there’s no way for a function satisfying \(y(t_0)=0\) to also satisfy the differential equation at \(t_0\) — the two conditions are simply incompatible, and no solution can exist.
Away from \(t=0\), we can integrate directly: for \(t>0\), \(\frac{dy}{dt}=1\), and for \(t<0\), \(\frac{dy}{dt}=-1\). Matching these to a common value \(y(0)=y_0\) forces \(y(t)=y_0+|t|\). But \(|t|\) has a corner at \(t=0\) and is not differentiable there, so no function can have derivative equal to \(\text{sign}(t)\) at \(t=0\) itself (since \(\text{sign}(0)\) isn’t even defined). This means there is no solution defined on any open interval containing \(t_0=0\).




Warning: If a solution exists, it does not necessarily mean it will be defined for all time!



Solve the initial value problem \[\frac{dy}{dt} = 1+y^2, \quad y(0)=0\]. Determine the interval of existence for \(y(t)\), i.e. the largest possible open interval \(I\) containing \(t=0\) on which the solution \(y(t)\) is defined.






TipAnswer:





Separating variables: \[\frac{1}{1+y^2}\,dy = dt \quad\Rightarrow\quad \arctan(y) = t+C\] Using \(y(0)=0\): \(\arctan(0)=0=0+C\), so \(C=0\). Solving for \(y\): \[y(t)=\tan(t)\] Since \(\tan(t)\) has vertical asymptotes at \(t=\pm\pi/2\), and \(t=0\) lies in between them, the largest open interval containing \(t=0\) on which \(y(t)=\tan(t)\) is defined (and satisfies the differential equation) is \[I = \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\] Even though the differential equation \(\frac{dy}{dt}=1+y^2\) itself is perfectly well-behaved for every real value of \(y\), the solution still cannot be extended past \(t=\pm\pi/2\) — it “runs away” to \(\pm\infty\) in finite time.

title: Existence & Uniqueness
text:
Uniqueness
The second question we have to address is whether or not a solution to an initial value problem is unique.
This is particularly important for mathematical modeling. If we are using a differential equation to try and predict how some real world system will evolve, we want to know that that our model predicts a unique outcome!
The following example illustrates how uniqueness can fail.

Problem 3: Uniqueness
Find at least two functions \(y(t)\) satisfying the initial value problem: \[\frac{dy}{dt}=y^{2/3}, \quad y(1)=0\].






TipAnswer:





One solution is the constant (equilibrium) solution \[y_1(t) = 0 \quad\text{for all } t\] since \(\frac{dy}{dt}=0\) and \(y^{2/3}=0^{2/3}=0\) agree, and \(y_1(1)=0\) as required.
A second solution can be found (away from \(y=0\)) by separating variables: \[y^{-2/3}\,dy = dt \quad\Rightarrow\quad 3y^{1/3} = t+C \quad\Rightarrow\quad y = \left(\frac{t+C}{3}\right)^3\] Using \(y(1)=0\) gives \(C=-1\), so \[y_2(t) = \left(\frac{t-1}{3}\right)^3\] You can check directly that \(y_2\) also satisfies both the differential equation and the initial condition. Since \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) are both valid solutions to the same initial value problem, this example shows that solutions to \(\frac{dy}{dt}=y^{2/3}\) are not unique — in fact, infinitely many other solutions (that follow \(y_1\) for a while, then “peel off” onto a shifted copy of \(y_2\)) exist as well!

title: Analyze & Interpret the Model
text: Once we have converted our question into a clearly stated, well-defined math problem, we can begin to analyze it.

title: Analyze & Interpret the Model
text:
Qualitative Approach - Slope Fields
Slope fields are one tool that we can use to try and understand the behavior of a solution \(y(t)\). To create a slope field for the equation \(\frac{dy}{dt}=f(t,y)\):

Select a grid of points in the \((t,y)\)-plane.
At each point \((t,y)\) in your grid, draw a small line through that point with slope \(f(t,y)\).
Each “slope” that you draw really represents a tangent line. Any solution passing through that point must be tangent to the line you draw at that point.
Once all your slopes are drawn, sit back and stare at it for a bit like a Magic Eye puzzle.

If \(f(t,y)\) isn’t too complicated, we can use the slope field to, either mentally or by hand, sketch out what a solution to the differential equation is going to look like. At the very least, try to see where a solution \(y(t)\) will be increasing/decreasing. You may also be able to see what happens to \(y(t)\) as \(t\to\infty\). Occasionally, you may even be able to guess formulas for simple solutions to the differential equation based on the slope field. (See below for an example of such a scenario.)






NoteExample - Slope Field





For example, the slope field for \(\frac{dy}{dt}=y-t\) is shown below:






Figure 1: Slope Field Example



Looking closely at the slope field, we can see that there is one particular line where all the slopes line up. This suggests that any solution starting on this line will stay on this line. The equation of that line is \(y=t+1\).
Is this actually a solution? Checking \(y(t)=t+1\): \[\begin{align}
& y'(t)=1 \\
& y(t)-t = t+1 - t = 1   
\end{align}\] We see that this satisfies the differential equation and is therefore a solution.
We can also see how other solutions will behave relative to the one we found. If a solution starts above the line \(y=t+1\), it will increase away from this line. If a solution starts just below \(y=t+1\), it will increase at first, but its slope will be less than 1 and so it will bend away from the line \(y=t+1\). Eventually, the solution will intersect the line \(y=t\), where all the values of \(dy/dt=0\); after this point, the solution will decrease.






Figure 2: Sketch of Solutions







Discussion Problem 1: Sprint Speed Continued
Recall that our model for a sprinter’s speed throughout a 100m race is given by: \[m\frac{dv}{dt}=mP-kmv\] where \(m\) is the sprinter’s mass (in kg), \(P\) represents the max effort acceleration a sprinter can achieve (in m/s\(^2\)), and \(k\) is the proportionality constant for the resistive force (in s\(^{-1}\)).
We will start by analyzing it qualitatively:

Describe how the sprinter’s speed is expected to change throughout the race according to the model. Will it increase? decrease?
Describe how the sprinter’s acceleration is expected to change throughout the race.
Sketch a graph of \(v(t)\). What do you expect to happen to \(v(t)\) in the long run, i.e. what is \[\lim_{t\to\infty}v(t)?\] What is the practical significance of this?







TipAnswer:





First, it helps to simplify the differential equation by dividing through by mass: \[\frac{dv}{dt}=P-kv\]

Note that \(\frac{dv}{dt}=0\) when \(v=\frac{P}{k}\). So, that means if the sprinter is ever going at this speed, they will stay at this speed for all time. A constant solution to a differential equation, like this one, is called a equilibrium solution.
If \(v>\frac{P}{k}\), then \(\frac{dv}{dt}<0\), and so at this speed, their speed will decrease.
If \(v<\frac{P}{k}\), then \(\frac{dv}{dt}>0\), and so at this speed, their speed will increase.
In context, their speed at the beginning of the race will be 0 and so this is telling us that their speed should increase throughout the race according to the model.
If \(v\) is increasing throughout the race, then their acceleration \[\frac{dv}{dt}=P-kv\] will decrease.
Here is a “sketch” of a solution using a slope or direction field.







Figure 3: Slope Field Sketch of Sprint Speed



This tells us that, as the race goes on, the runner’s speed will approach a threshold of \(P/k\). This tells us that, if a runner is looking to improve their performance, they need to figure out how to make \(P\) bigger or \(k\) smaller.

title: Analyze & Interpret the Model
text:
Numerical Approach - Euler’s Method
When sketching solutions using a slope field, we start at a particular point, then move forward by allowing the slopes to “push” the solution in a particular direction. Euler’s method makes this idea a little more precise by turning it in to a sequence of computations.
The main idea—to approximate a solution \(y(t)\) for the differential equation \[\frac{dy}{dt}=f(t,y):\]

Choose \((t_0, y_0)\), the starting point in the \((t,y)\)-plane. If you are solving an initial value problem, use the indicated starting point.
Specify an ending time \(t_N>t_0\).
Choose \(N\), the total number of steps you will be using to get from \(t_0\) to \(t_N\).
Use linear approximation to recursively generate a sequence of estimates \(y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_N\) for the values \(y(t_1), y(t_2), \ldots, y(t_N)\).
The piecewise linear function defined by the points \((t_0, y_0), (t_1,y_1), \ldots, (t_N,y_N)\) is then your approximation for the solution \(y(t)\) on the interval \(t_0\leq t\leq t_N\).







NoteExample - Euler’s Method





For example, we can apply this idea to approximate the solution of \[\frac{dy}{dt}=y-t\] on the interval \(0\leq t \leq 2\), assuming that \(y(0)=0.5\). Using four steps (\(N=4\)):

The graph below shows how the approximate solution (black) compares to the actual solution (red). The green curve illustrates the improvement in the approximate solution when we increase the number of steps used by a factor of 10.






Figure 4: Approximate Solutions from Euler’s Method






This process can be stated more formally as follows:

Definition 1 (Euler’s Method) To create an approximate solution for the initial value problem \[\frac{dy}{dt}=f(t,y), \quad y(t_0)=y_0 \] on the interval \(t_0\leq t\leq t_N\):
Initialization: Choose \(N\), the number of steps that will be used in the approximation. This determines the time step for each step of the procedure, \(\Delta t = \frac{t_N-t_0}{N}\). The initial value \(y(t_0)=y_0\) and time interval for the approximate solution \(t_0\leq t\leq t_N\) may also need to be chosen if not given by the problem.
Computations: For \(k=1,\ldots N\), we approximate the value of \(y(t_k)\) by \[y(t_k)\approx y_k = y_{k-1}+f(t_{k-1},y_{k-1})\cdot \Delta t, \quad\text{where } t_k=t_{k-1}+\Delta t\]
Final Output: Once the \(y_k\) are computed, the approximate solution \(\widetilde{y}(t)\) is the piecewise linear function on \(t_0\leq t\leq t_N\) connecting the points \((t_k, y_k)\); that is, for \(k=1,\ldots N\), on the \(k\)-th subinterval: \[\widetilde{y}(t)=y_{k-1}+f(t_{k-1},y_{k-1})\cdot(t-t_{k-1}), \quad\text{for } t_{k-1}\leq t\leq t_k\]

title: Analyze & Interpret the Model
text:
Analytical Approach - Separation of Variables
The method of separation of variables is an example of one technique we can use to try and find formulas for solutions to differential equations. This technique only works on separable equations, that is equations that can be separated as the product of a function in \(t\) and a function in \(y\): \[\frac{dy}{dt} = f(t,y) = g(t)h(y)\]
The steps in this method are:

Separate. Move things around so that you have your \(y\) terms and \(t\) terms on separate sides of the equation \[\frac{1}{h(y)}dy = g(t)dt \]
Integrate. Find general antiderivatives for both sides of the equation. Since the constants of integration can be combined, we generally only write “+ C” on the time side: \[\int\frac{1}{h(y)}dy =\int g(t)dt \Rightarrow H(y) = G(t) + C \]
Isolate. Use algebra to get \(y\) by itself. \[y(t)= H^{-1}(G(t)+C)\]
Initial Condition. For initial value problems, substitute the initial condition \((t_0, y_0)\) into the equation in order to solve for \(C\).


Discussion Problem 3: Analytical Analysis.
Our model for how sprint speed will change throughout the race:

Use separation of variables this technique to solve the equation.
Once you have your general solution, try and solve the initial value problem, where we are looking for a solution to the equation such that \(v(0)=0\).







TipAnswer:






Starting again from \(\frac{dv}{dt}=P-kv\), we separate variables: \[\frac{1}{P-kv}\,dv = dt\] Integrating both sides (folding the constant of integration into the time side): \[-\frac{1}{k}\ln|P-kv| = t+C\] Solving for \(v\): \[|P-kv| = e^{-k(t+C)} = e^{-kC}e^{-kt}\] Since \(e^{-kC}\) is just some positive constant, we can drop the absolute value by allowing our constant to take either sign: \[P-kv = Be^{-kt} \quad\Rightarrow\quad v(t) = \frac{P}{k}-\frac{B}{k}e^{-kt}\] Renaming \(B/k\) as our arbitrary constant \(A\), our general solution is \[v(t) = \frac{P}{k}-Ae^{-kt}\]
Using the initial condition \(v(0)=0\): \[0 = \frac{P}{k}-A \quad\Rightarrow\quad A=\frac{P}{k}\] So the solution to our initial value problem is \[v(t) = \frac{P}{k}\left(1-e^{-kt}\right)\] Notice that as \(t\to\infty\), \(v(t)\to P/k\) — exactly what we predicted using our qualitative approach back in Discussion Problem 1!

Note that each one did not immediately start running. The first recorded time is their reaction time \(t_0\). How can this be factored into our model?
The data from the race compares distance vs. time. Using your answer to Problem 3b, find a formula for the distance a sprinter had run, \(x(t)\) (in m), \(t\) seconds into the race for \(t>t_0\).
Alfred’s reaction time was \(0.14\)s and Lyles’ was \(0.18\)s. Their race data has been loaded into Desmos here. Using your general formula for \(x(t)\) and the curve fitting tool in Desmos, determine the values of \(P\) and \(k\) that best fit the data.







TipAnswer:






Our model assumes the sprinter starts running (i.e. \(v=0\) and accelerating according to our equation) at \(t=0\). In reality, each sprinter’s clock starts at the gun, but they don’t begin accelerating until their reaction time \(t_0\) has elapsed. We can account for this by shifting our solution in time: it’s valid starting at \(t=t_0\) rather than \(t=0\), so wherever \(t\) appears in our formula from Discussion Problem 3b, we should use \(t-t_0\) (the time since the sprinter started running) in its place.
Since \(x(t) = \int v(t)\,dt\), and (using our answer to part a) \(v(t) = \dfrac{P}{k}\left(1-e^{-k(t-t_0)}\right)\) for \(t>t_0\), with \(x(t_0)=0\): \[x(t) = \int_{t_0}^{t}\frac{P}{k}\left(1-e^{-k(s-t_0)}\right)\,ds = \frac{P}{k}(t-t_0) - \frac{P}{k}\left[-\frac{1}{k}e^{-k(s-t_0)}\right]_{t_0}^{t}\] \[x(t) = \frac{P}{k}(t-t_0) - \frac{P}{k^2}\left(1-e^{-k(t-t_0)}\right), \quad t>t_0\]
Plugging each sprinter’s reaction time \(t_0\) into the formula from part b and using Desmos’s curve-fitting/regression tool against the \((t,x)\) data provided, you should be able to obtain a best-fit pair of values \((P,k)\) for each sprinter. Since the exact fitted values depend on the details of your regression setup, you may not get precisely the same numbers as your classmates — but you should find that Lyles’ fitted values produce a larger terminal velocity \(P/k\) than Alfred’s, consistent with him running the faster of the two races.

title: Modeling with Differential Equations
text: To introduce the course, we are going to start with an example that illustrates the process for modeling relationships between variables with differential equations. Before diving into our example, two questions need to be addressed:

title: Modeling with Differential Equations
text:
What will we study?
What is new in this class is that the kinds of differential equations we want to solve will depend explicitly on the dependent variable. Our focus will be on ordinary differential equations (ODEs); ODEs can involve multiple dependent variables, however, they depend only on a single independent variable, usually thought of as time.
Equations where there are multiple independent variables (e.g. time and space) will involve partial derivatives, which is the focus of MATH-451 Partial Differential Equations (or PDEs).
We will start out with first-order equations, those that involve only the first derivative, and can be written in the form:

Definition 1 (First-Order Equations) Find \(y:I\subseteq\mathbb R\to \mathbb R\) (or maybe \(\mathbb C\)) such that
\[\frac{dy}{dt}=f(t,y)\] for all \(t\) in the interval \(I\).

Later on, we will discuss first-order systems, which will involve several dependent variables, each with an equation for its derivative. We can write these systems succinctly in vector form in terms of a vector-valued function \(\mathbf{v}(t)\):

Definition 2 (First-Order Systems) Find \(\mathbf{v}: I\subseteq\mathbb R\to \mathbb R^n\) (or maybe \(\mathbb C^n\)) such that \[\frac{d\mathbf{v}}{dt}=f(t,\mathbf{v})\] for all \(t\) in the interval \(I\).

We will also discuss second-order equations (and maybe a few second-order systems), which add second derivatives into the mix:

Definition 3 (Second-Order Equations) Find \(y:I\subseteq\mathbb R \to \mathbb R\) (or maybe \(\mathbb C\)) such that \[\frac{d^2y}{dt^2}=f\left(t,y,\frac{dy}{dt}\right)\] for all \(t\) in the interval \(I\).

title: First Order Equations
text:
Our first unit covers chapter 1 of our textbook, along with some topics from sections 7.1-3 and Appendices A and B.
Key Ideas:

Basic terminology associated with differential equations
Using differential equations to model relationships between variables
Three main approaches to analyzing differential equations: qualitative, numerical, and analytical

Qualitative approach for first-order equations:

Slope fields and Phase lines
Equilibria, stability, and bifurcation diagrams.

Numerical approach for first-order equations:

Euler’s method
Error & improvements on Euler’s method (Improved Euler’s method, Runge-Kutta)

Analytical approach for first-order equations:

Existence and uniqueness criteria
Separation of variables
Integrating factors
Change of variables, power series, other techniques as time allows

title: Analyze & Interpret the Model
text: Once we have converted our question into a clearly stated, well-defined math problem, we can begin to analyze it.

title: Analyze & Interpret the Model
text:
Qualitative Approach - Slope Fields
Slope fields are one tool that we can use to try and understand the behavior of a solution \(y(t)\) and describe it qualitatively.

Definition 1 (Slope Field) To create a slope field (also called a direction field) for the equation \(\frac{dy}{dt}=f(t,y)\):

Choose Grid: Select a grid of points in the \((t,y)\)-plane. You want your grid to be dense enough to be informative, but not overcrowded.

Draw Slopes: At each point \((t,y)\) in your grid, draw a small line through that point with slope \(f(t,y)\). Each line that you draw should be roughly the same length. Choose this length so that it is easy to read how the slope changes throughout the \((t,y)\)-plane, but not so long that they overlap.
Sketch Solutions: Once all your slopes are drawn, sit back and stare at it for a bit like a Magic Eye puzzle. Each slope really represents a tangent line. Any solution to the differential equation passing through a grid point must be tangent to the line drawn at that point. So, we can use the slope field to sketch out what a solution to the differential equation is going to look like and begin to see some of its properties.


If \(f(t,y)\) isn’t too complicated, we may be able to guess formulas for simple solutions to the differential equation based on the slope field. (See example below.)
At the very least, we can try to identify where a solution \(y(t)\) will be increasing/decreasing and try to determine its end behavior. That is what happens to \(y(t)\) in the long-run as time moves forwards (or backwards).






NoteExample - Slope Field





For example, the slope field for \(\frac{dy}{dt}=y-t\) is shown below:






Figure 1: Slope Field Example



Looking closely at the slope field, we can see that there is one particular line where all the slopes line up. This suggests that any solution starting on this line will stay on this line. The equation of that line is \(y=t+1\).
Is this actually a solution? Checking \(y(t)=t+1\): \[\begin{align}
& y'(t)=1 \\
& y(t)-t = t+1 - t = 1   
\end{align}\] We see that this satisfies the differential equation and is therefore a solution.
We can also see how other solutions will behave relative to the one we found. If a solution starts above the line \(y=t+1\), it will increase away from this line. If a solution starts just below \(y=t+1\), it will increase at first, but its slope will be less than 1 and so it will bend away from the line \(y=t+1\). Eventually, the solution will intersect the line \(y=t\), where all the values of \(dy/dt=0\); after this point, the solution will decrease.






Figure 2: Sketch of Solutions







Discussion Problem 1: Sprint Speed Continued
Recall that our model for a sprinter’s speed throughout a 100m race is given by: \[m\frac{dv}{dt}=mP-kmv\] where \(m\) is the sprinter’s mass (in kg), \(P\) represents the max effort acceleration a sprinter can achieve (in m/s\(^2\)), and \(k\) is the proportionality constant for the resistive force (in s\(^{-1}\)).
Create a slope field for this differential equation and use it to help you answer the following:

Describe how the sprinter’s speed is expected to change throughout the race according to the model. Will it increase? decrease? remain constant?
Describe how the sprinter’s acceleration is expected to change throughout the race.
Sketch a graph of \(v(t)\). What do you expect to happen to \(v(t)\) in the long run, i.e. what is \[\lim_{t\to\infty}v(t)?\] What is the practical significance of this?







TipAnswer:





First, it helps to simplify the differential equation by dividing through by mass: \[\frac{dv}{dt}=P-kv\]

Note that \(\frac{dv}{dt}=0\) when \(v=\frac{P}{k}\). So, that means if the sprinter is ever going at this speed, they will stay at this speed for all time. A constant solution to a differential equation, like this one, is called a equilibrium solution.
If \(v>\frac{P}{k}\), then \(\frac{dv}{dt}<0\), and so at this speed, their speed will decrease.
If \(v<\frac{P}{k}\), then \(\frac{dv}{dt}>0\), and so at this speed, their speed will increase.
In context, their speed at the beginning of the race will be 0 and so this is telling us that their speed should increase throughout the race according to the model.
If \(v\) is increasing throughout the race, then their acceleration \[\frac{dv}{dt}=P-kv\] will decrease.
Here is a “sketch” of a solution using a slope or direction field.







Figure 3: Slope Field Sketch of Sprint Speed



This tells us that, as the race goes on, the runner’s speed will approach a threshold of \(P/k\). This tells us that, if a runner is looking to improve their performance, they need to figure out how to make \(P\) bigger or \(k\) smaller.

title: Analyze & Interpret the Model
text:
Numerical Approach - Euler’s Method
When sketching solutions using a slope field, we start at a particular point \((t_0, y_0)\), then move forward (or backward) by allowing the slopes to “push” the solution in a particular direction. Euler’s method makes this idea a little more precise by turning it in to a sequence of computations.
The main idea—to approximate a solution \(y(t)\) for the differential equation \[\frac{dy}{dt}=f(t,y):\]

Choose \((t_0, y_0)\), the starting point in the \((t,y)\)-plane. If you are solving an initial value problem, this initial point is given in the problem.
Specify an ending time \(t_N>t_0\).

Choose \(N\), the total number of steps you will be using to get from \(t_0\) to \(t_N\).
Use linear approximation to recursively generate a sequence of estimates \(y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_N\) for the values \(y(t_1), y(t_2), \ldots, y(t_N)\).
The piecewise linear function defined by the points \((t_0, y_0), (t_1,y_1), \ldots, (t_N,y_N)\) is then your approximation for the solution \(y(t)\) on the interval \(t_0\leq t\leq t_N\).







NoteExample - Euler’s Method





For example, we can apply this idea to approximate the solution of \[\frac{dy}{dt}=y-t\] on the interval \(0\leq t \leq 2\), assuming that \(y(0)=0.5\). Using four steps (\(N=4\)):

Figure 4: Approximate Solutions from Euler’s Method






This process can be stated more formally as follows:

Definition 2 (Euler’s Method) To create an approximate solution for the initial value problem \[\frac{dy}{dt}=f(t,y), \quad y(t_0)=y_0 \] on the interval \(t_0\leq t\leq t_N\):
Initialization: Choose \(N\), the number of steps that will be used in the approximation. This determines the time step for each step of the procedure, \(\Delta t = \frac{t_N-t_0}{N}\). The initial value \(y(t_0)=y_0\) and time interval for the approximate solution \(t_0\leq t\leq t_N\) may also need to be chosen if not given by the problem.
Computations: For \(k=1,\ldots N\), we approximate the value of \(y(t_k)\) by \[y(t_k)\approx y_k = y_{k-1}+f(t_{k-1},y_{k-1})\cdot \Delta t, \quad\text{where } t_k=t_{k-1}+\Delta t\]
Final Output: Once the \(y_k\) are computed, the approximate solution \(\widetilde{y}(t)\) is the piecewise linear function on \(t_0\leq t\leq t_N\) connecting the points \((t_k, y_k)\); that is, for \(k=1,\ldots N\), on the \(k\)-th subinterval: \[\widetilde{y}(t)=y_{k-1}+f(t_{k-1},y_{k-1})\cdot(t-t_{k-1}), \quad\text{for } t_{k-1}\leq t\leq t_k\]

title: Analyze & Interpret the Model
text:
Analytical Approach - Separation of Variables
The method of separation of variables is an example of one technique we can use to try and find formulas for solutions to differential equations.

Definition 3 (Separation of Variables) If a differential equation is separable, that is, it can be written as the product of a function in \(t\) and a function in \(y\) \[ \frac{dy}{dt}=f(t,y)=g(t)h(y), \] then we can use the following method to try and find a formula for a solution:

Separate. Move things around so that you have your \(y\) terms and \(t\) terms on separate sides of the equation \[\frac{1}{h(y)}dy = g(t)dt \]
Integrate. Find general antiderivatives for both sides of the equation. Since the constants of integration can be combined, we generally only write “+ C” on the time side: \[\int\frac{1}{h(y)}dy =\int g(t)dt \Rightarrow H(y) = G(t) + C \]
Isolate. Use algebra to get \(y\) by itself. \[y(t)= H^{-1}(G(t)+C)\]
Solve for C. For initial value problems, substitute the initial condition \((t_0, y_0)\) into the equation in order to solve for \(C\).


The step where we separate the variables should look odd. We are treating \(\frac{dy}{dt}\) as a fraction when it is not. This algebraic maneuvering is really shorthand for manipulations that are based on the chain rule. See the explanation below if you want more details.






NoteExplanation - Separation Step





Recall that when you see \(y\) in the differential equation, it is a function of \(t\). In the separation step, what is really going on is that we are rewriting the equation as \[ \frac{1}{h(y(t))}\cdot y'(t)= g(t) \] When integrating the left-hand side, we use a change of variables and let \(u=y(t)\). Then, we have: \[ \int \frac{1}{h(y(t))}y'(t)\,dt = \int \frac{1}{h(u)}\,du\]



The method doesn’t always work. For example:

We are assuming \(h(y)\neq 0\) when we separate. If \(h(y)\) can equal 0, we may be ignoring some solutions.
We may not be able to find a closed-form antiderivative when we integrate either side.
We may not be able to isolate \(y\) and end up with an equation defining an implicit relationship between \(y\) and \(t\).


Discussion Problem 3: Analytical Analysis.
Our model for how sprint speed will change throughout the race: \[\frac{dv}{dt}=P-kv\]

Use separation of variables this technique to solve the equation.
Once you have your general solution, try and solve the initial value problem, where we are looking for a solution to the equation such that \(v(0)=0\).







TipAnswer:






Starting again from \(\frac{dv}{dt}=P-kv\), we separate variables: \[\frac{1}{P-kv}\,dv = dt\] Integrating both sides (folding the constant of integration into the time side): \[-\frac{1}{k}\ln|P-kv| = t+C\] Solving for \(v\): \[|P-kv| = e^{-k(t+C)} = e^{-kC}e^{-kt}\] Since \(e^{-kC}\) is just some positive constant, we can drop the absolute value by allowing our constant to take either sign: \[P-kv = Be^{-kt} \quad\Rightarrow\quad v(t) = \frac{P}{k}-\frac{B}{k}e^{-kt}\] Renaming \(B/k\) as our arbitrary constant \(A\), our general solution is \[v(t) = \frac{P}{k}-Ae^{-kt}\]
Using the initial condition \(v(0)=0\): \[0 = \frac{P}{k}-A \quad\Rightarrow\quad A=\frac{P}{k}\] So the solution to our initial value problem is \[v(t) = \frac{P}{k}\left(1-e^{-kt}\right)\] Notice that as \(t\to\infty\), \(v(t)\to P/k\) — exactly what we predicted using our qualitative approach back in Discussion Problem 1!

The data from the race compares distance vs. time. Using your answer to Problem 3b, find a formula for the distance a sprinter had run, \(x(t)\) (in m), \(t\) seconds into the race for \(t>t_0\).
Alfred’s reaction time was \(0.14\)s and Lyles’ was \(0.18\)s. Their race data has been loaded into Desmos here. Using your general formula for \(x(t)\) and the curve fitting tool in Desmos, determine the values of \(P\) and \(k\) that best fit the data.







TipAnswer:






To factor in reaction time, we can adjust the initial condition. So, if the runner actually starts running at \(t_0>0\), we look for the solution such that \(y(t_0)=0\). This is equivalent to shifting the solution we found in Problem 2 by \(t_0\): \[v(t)= \dfrac{P}{k}\left(1-e^{-k(t-t_0)}\right)\]
Since \(x(t) = \int v(t)\,dt\), and (using our answer to part a) \(v(t) = \dfrac{P}{k}\left(1-e^{-k(t-t_0)}\right)\) for \(t>t_0\), with \(x(t_0)=0\): \[x(t) = \int_{t_0}^{t}\frac{P}{k}\left(1-e^{-k(s-t_0)}\right)\,ds = \frac{P}{k}(t-t_0) - \frac{P}{k}\left[-\frac{1}{k}e^{-k(s-t_0)}\right]_{t_0}^{t}\] \[x(t) = \frac{P}{k}(t-t_0) - \frac{P}{k^2}\left(1-e^{-k(t-t_0)}\right), \quad t>t_0\]
Plugging each sprinter’s reaction time \(t_0\) into the formula from part b and using Desmos’s curve-fitting/regression tool against the \((t,x)\) data provided, you should be able to obtain a best-fit pair of values \((P,k)\) for each sprinter. The model fits the data fairly well. Look for any points that appear more off than others and try to think about what may have caused the deviation.

title: Existence & Uniqueness
text:
Before analyzing an initial value problem (IVP) \[\frac{dy}{dt}=f(t,y), \quad y(t_0)=y_0\]
qualitatively or numerically, it is important to know the answer to two analytic questions:

title: Existence & Uniqueness
text:
Uniqueness
The second question we have to address is whether or not a solution to an initial value problem is unique.
This is particularly important for mathematical modeling. If we are using a differential equation to try and predict how some real world system will evolve, we want to know that that our model predicts a unique outcome!
The following example illustrates how uniqueness can fail.

Problem 3: Uniqueness
Find at least two functions \(y(t)\) satisfying the initial value problem: \[\frac{dy}{dt}=y^{2/3}, \quad y(1)=0\].






TipAnswer:





One solution is the constant (equilibrium) solution \[y_1(t) = 0 \quad\text{for all } t\] since \(\frac{dy}{dt}=0\) and \(y^{2/3}=0^{2/3}=0\) agree, and \(y_1(1)=0\) as required.
A second solution can be found (away from \(y=0\)) by separating variables: \[y^{-2/3}\,dy = dt \quad\Rightarrow\quad 3y^{1/3} = t+C \quad\Rightarrow\quad y = \left(\frac{t+C}{3}\right)^3\] Using \(y(1)=0\) gives \(C=-1\), so \[y_2(t) = \left(\frac{t-1}{3}\right)^3\] You can check directly that \(y_2\) also satisfies both the differential equation and the initial condition. Since \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) are both valid solutions to the same initial value problem, this example shows that solutions to \(\frac{dy}{dt}=y^{2/3}\) are not unique — in fact, infinitely many other solutions (that follow \(y_1\) for a while, then “peel off” onto a shifted copy of \(y_2\)) exist as well!

title: Existence & Uniqueness
text:
Footnotes


An interval is open if it doesn’t include its endpoints; i.e. it can be written as \((a,b)\) or \(a<t<b\) where \(a\) and \(b\) are either values or \(\pm\infty\).↩︎

title: Slope Fields, Phase Lines, and Bifurcations
text:
Suppose you lost power inside your home and the temperature inside the building is changing as heat is exchanged through the exterior of the building.
Let \(H\) be the temperature inside your home and \(E\) be the temperature outside your home. Assume that:

The external temperature \(E\) is constant.
The rate of change of the temperature inside your home is proportional to the difference between the external and internal temperatures.

Based on these assumptions:

Write a differential equation modeling the rate of change of the temperature inside of your home.
Sketch the slope field for this differential equation.
Explain the different scenarios for how \(H(t)\) is expected to change as \(t\to\infty\).
Explain how you are implicitly using the Existence and Uniqueness theorems in your conclusions for part (c).
Now suppose \(E\) is not constant but fluctuates sinusoidally over time, e.g. \[E(t)=A\sin(k(t-T))+E_T\] what effect does this have on the long-term behavior of \(H(t)\)? Again, use a slope field to help you make your guess. Here is a link to a Desmos graph you can modify to help you make your conclusions.

title: Slope Fields, Phase Lines, and Bifurcations
text:
Autonomous Systems - Phase Lines

Problem 2: Population Growth
In the absence of external factors, a simple model for how a population size \(P\) evolves over time is to assume that it changes at a rate proportional to its size. Another way of saying this is to assume that the relative growth rate of the population is constant.

Write the differential equation modeling the rate of change of the population assuming its relative growth rate is constant. How will \(P\) change over time under this assumption?
Ignoring external factors is not very realistic in the long-run. As the population grows, resources will be scarcer (food, shelter, etc.) and this will impact the growth rate. So, to make our model more realistic, we can assume that the relative growth rate starts initially (when \(P\) is close to 0) at some intrinsic growth rate \(r\), but then decreases linearly with respect to the population size.
The relative growth rate will become 0 as the population size approaches some threshold \(N\) determined by the limits of the surrounding environment to support the population. This parameter is often called the carrying capacity for the environment.

Write a differential equation modeling the rate of change of the population under these assumptions.
Find all equilibrium solutions for the equation. Use a phase line to analyze their stability.
In general, how do we expect the population size \(P\) to change under these assumptions?

Other external factors can also impact the growth rate of a population. For example, consider our previous model, and now assume that the population is something that is harvested for food by humans (e.g. blue crabs in the Chesapeake Bay). Lets assume that the species is harvested at a rate of \(H\) individuals per unit time (where \(H\) is a constant that is set by a regulatory agency).

Adapt your model from part (b) to include the harvesting rate \(H\).
How will the equilibria and their stability depend on \(H\)?
